context: In each of the four panels, orange node 3 is the unbalanced node to repair. The blue node is its child on the taller side. The green node shows the direction in which the subtree continues. A gray rounded rectangle encloses the unbalanced subtree that needs a rotation.

The balance factor f is the left subtree height minus the right subtree height. For each case, the table lists f for unbalanced node 3 and for its child on the taller side so you can check the choice of rotation.
description: The four cases before rotation appear from left to right. The first two have overall root 4, right child 5, and an unbalanced left subtree rooted at 3. The last two have overall root 2, left child 1, and an unbalanced right subtree rooted at 3. The table summarizes the four local configurations and the rotations labeled beneath them. Names such as “left-left” describe the directions of two successive branches. Node values, edges, and rotation methods come from the figure. The balance factors are calculated using height 0 for a leaf and −1 for an empty subtree. They are not labeled in the figure.

frames.explanation: The general rule from the text is as follows. If the unbalanced node has f > 1, check its left child. If the child's f ≥ 0, rotate right. If its f < 0, rotate the left child left, then the unbalanced node right. If the unbalanced node has f < −1, check its right child. If the child's f ≤ 0, rotate left. If its f > 0, rotate the right child right, then the unbalanced node left. The general rule includes a child with f = 0, which can occur after deletion, for example.
frames.title: Four AVL imbalances and how to choose a rotation

result: A chain that leans in one direction needs a single rotation. For a path that bends back, rotate the child first and then the unbalanced node. The inorder sequence stays the same.
summary: Four local tree shapes before rotation call for one of two repairs: a single or a double rotation.
